title: Tomorrow’s weather written high up
teaches: It’s sunny today: how do you spot rain 12 to 24 hours before it comes? Mares’ tails and contrails, the 22° halo of cirrostratus, the frosted glass of altostratus, and a warm front’s countdown from first cirrus to rain

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: High cloud rides far out ahead of a storm. Cirrus that spreads and thickens from the west is often the first sign of rain a day away.
Contrails are a gauge of the high air: short ones that vanish mean it is dry, and fair weather is holding; long ones that spread into a sheet mean it is moist, as it is ahead of a storm.
A ring 22° round the sun or moon, about a spread hand-span, means a thin veil of ice crystals: **cirrostratus**.
When the sun turns to a dim disc, as if behind frosted glass, and shadows vanish, the sheet is **altostratus**. When the sun is gone without a trace, it is Lesson 2’s nimbostratus.
The countdown of a warm front: cirrus, then a halo (rain within 12 to 24 hours), then frosted glass (rain within a few hours), then rain.

blocks.text: This lesson heads up to the high floor. Its clouds look thin and delicate, and they give the earliest weather warnings you can get from the ground: on a bright, sunny day, the high sky can already be telling you about tomorrow’s rain.

Climb high enough and the air stays below freezing even on a summer afternoon. On a mild 15 °C (59 °F) day in the valley, the air is around −24 °C by six kilometres up and below −50 °C near the top of the weather. Up there, cloud is ice. (Water can stay liquid well below freezing on the way up, which matters a great deal for rain; that is Lesson 7.)

Up on the high floor, ice crystals form distinct clouds of their own. **Cirrus** consists of shafts of falling ice crystals. When crystals nucleate in a moist pocket near the top of the troposphere, they quickly grow to a tenth of a millimetre or more across (at least ten times the width of a typical liquid droplet) and fall at roughly half a metre to a metre per second. As the crystals descend into lower layers, they encounter air moving at different speeds. Because surface friction slows the wind near the ground while air high aloft flows unimpeded, wind speed usually changes with altitude, a variation known as **wind shear**. As falling crystals drop into slower-moving air below, they lag behind the faster-moving source pocket above, drawing the falling streak out into a long, curved trail.

blocks.caption: Ice crystals falling from a moist patch high up.
blocks.task: Add wind shear until the trails curl into hooks.

blocks.text: Those hooked, comma-shaped streaks are known as **mares’ tails**. The tufted head of the hook marks the pocket where new ice crystals are forming, while the long, trailing tail shows the crystals falling through wind shear and slowly sublimating back into water vapour in drier air below. Because ice crystals are much larger and far sparser than liquid cloud droplets (often fewer than one crystal for every thousand droplets in a low cloud), cirrus clouds look fibrous and silky, letting plenty of blue sky show through.

Aeroplanes give you a second gauge of the high air. A contrail is cloud made by the engines: their exhaust is full of water vapour, which mixes with air at −40 °C or colder and freezes at once into a line of ice crystals. Whether the line lasts depends on the air it is drawn in. **Short contrails** that vanish a little way behind the plane mean the high air is dry: the ice evaporates as fast as it forms, and fair weather is holding. **Long contrails** that linger, widen and fan out into a sheet mean the air up there is already close to full of vapour, as it is far out ahead of a storm.

Watch what the cirrus does over the next few hours. A few wisps that drift over and stay a few wisps mean little. Cirrus that keeps spreading in from the west, thickening and joining up into a milky sheet, is the leading edge of a storm’s cloud.

That milky sheet often wears a ring. Many high ice crystals grow as tiny six-sided columns or plates, like short lengths of a pencil. Light that enters one side face and leaves by the next-but-one passes through a 60° wedge of ice, a prism, and is bent by at least about 22°; over a wide range of tilts it is bent by very nearly 22°, so the light piles up at that angle. Among millions of crystals tumbling at random, the ones that sit 22° from the sun, as you look, are the ones that bend their light into your eye, and together they draw a circle.

blocks.caption: Crystals all over the sky, each turned at random. The bright ones are sending light to your eye.
blocks.task: Add crystals until the ring appears.

blocks.text: That bright ring is the **22° halo**. The sky just inside the ring looks noticeably darker than the sky outside it because no ray passing through a 60° ice prism can be bent by less than the minimum angle, leaving a sharp inner boundary. That inner edge is tinted faintly red: ice slows red light slightly less than blue light, so red light has a minimum deflection of about 21.5° while blue light bends by at least 22.4°. Red light therefore forms the innermost rim of the circle, while the other colours overlap further out and blend back into white. On the sky, a 22° radius is quite large: if you stretch your arm out straight and spread your fingers wide, the distance from the sun to the halo spans roughly from the tip of your thumb to the tip of your little finger.

Because only hexagonal ice crystals produce a 22° ring, and forming a complete circle requires crystals distributed evenly across the sky, a full halo is the signature of **cirrostratus**. Cirrostratus is a thin, milky veil of ice crystals covering the sky, translucent enough that the sun’s outline stays sharp and objects on the ground still cast clear shadows. Whether a cirrostratus halo is harmless or a warning depends on how the sky changes over the next few hours.

**Altostratus** is the smooth, featureless sheet of the middle floor, forming a grey or bluish-grey layer of mixed water droplets and ice crystals that often covers the entire sky. It is too thick for you to see the sharp outline of the sun, yet thin enough in places for the sun to shine through faintly as a pale disc, as if viewed through frosted glass.

blocks.caption: The sun behind thin, thicker and very thick cloud.

blocks.text: Two simple checks distinguish altostratus from thinner or thicker sheets. First, under altostratus, **shadows vanish**. Because the cloud deck scatters sunlight thoroughly, most of the light reaching the ground comes evenly from the entire overcast sky rather than in a direct beam from the sun, illuminating objects from all sides and filling in shadows.

Second, altostratus produces **no halo** around the sun. An optical halo forms when ice crystals bend sunlight by a fixed angle (22°), which only stays visible in a thin ice veil where a ray of sunlight passes through a single crystal on its way to your eye. In a deep altostratus deck containing both droplets and ice, each light ray is scattered repeatedly from particle to particle in new directions, scrambling any 22° ring into an even glow.

Thicker still, and even the pale disc goes: the sun’s position vanishes entirely, the base blurs into falling rain, and the sheet has become Lesson 2’s **nimbostratus**. So the sun itself is the gauge. A sharp sun with shadows and perhaps a halo: cirrostratus. A dim disc and no shadows: altostratus. No sun at all: nimbostratus.

parts.title: A warm front, from far off

blocks.text: Middle-floor clouds usually form a different way: by broad, gentle lifting, as a wide layer of moist air glides slowly upward over hundreds of kilometres. This happens most often out in front of a storm. That word needs some care, because it is used for two very different things.

The storm most people picture is a **thunderstorm**: a single towering cloud (cumulonimbus) a few kilometres across, built by warm air bubbling straight up from the ground, usually on a hot afternoon. It grows in an hour, pours for less than an hour and drifts on. A thunderstorm is a heap cloud from Lesson 1 grown enormous, and it gets the next lesson to itself.

The other kind is a **frontal storm**, the kind behind a long grey day of steady rain or snow. It is not one cloud but a whole weather system, often a thousand kilometres across, that takes a day or two to pass over. At its heart, a mass of warm, moist air runs into a mass of colder air. Cold air is denser, so it stays low and hugs the ground as a long, thin wedge, and the warm air does not push it aside but slides up over the top of it. The line on the ground where the two meet is called a **front**.

Across the mid-latitudes, huge air masses hundreds of kilometres wide move across the continent, some carrying warm, moist air from lower latitudes and others bringing cool, denser air from closer to the poles. When an advancing mass of warm air overtakes a retreating wedge of cold air, the boundary between them is called a **warm front**. Because the warm air is less dense than the cold air ahead of it, it cannot easily shove the heavy cold air out of the way; instead, it glides up and over the cold wedge along a very gentle slope, rising only about one kilometre vertically for every hundred kilometres horizontally.

blocks.caption: A frontal storm seen side-on: warm air gliding up over a wedge of cold air.

blocks.text: As the warm, moist air glides up that gradual ramp, it expands and cools across a region hundreds of kilometres wide, forming broad cloud sheets at every level along the slope. Because the frontal slope is roughly 1 in 100, the top of the ramp at an altitude of ten kilometres sits nearly a thousand kilometres ahead of the surface boundary where the front touches the ground. To an observer on the ground, an approaching warm front arrives backwards from top to bottom: you see its highest ice clouds first, followed by progressively lower and thicker layers as the wedge of cold air retreats. Since a typical warm front advances at around 25 kilometres per hour, those first high cirrus streaks can appear overhead a day and a half before the surface front arrives.

blocks.caption: A warm front, moving towards you at about 25 km/h.
blocks.task: Let the front come in until rain is about to arrive.

blocks.text: This top-down progression gives you a reliable timeline from the ground: detached **cirrus** hooks invading from one side of the horizon, thickening into a milky **cirrostratus** veil with a 22° halo, lowering and greying into **altostratus** that dims the sun into a frosted disc and washes out the halo, and finally deepening into an overcast rain deck.

Rain begins well before the surface front reaches you, as soon as the cloud deck overhead grows deep enough to span from the ice-growth zone down to the lower sky, typically across the last two or three hundred kilometres ahead of the surface boundary. From the time you first spot a halo in thickening cirrostratus, steady rain usually arrives within **12 to 24 hours**; once altostratus has hidden the sharp disc of the sun, rain is only a few hours away.

Moonlight refracts through cirrostratus at the exact same 22° angle at night, which is where the old saying 'ring around the moon, rain soon' comes from. Sometimes a high veil passes by without a full front behind it, but when the veil keeps thickening, the old rhyme holds up well.

The old rhyme “red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning” has the same root. Our weather comes from the west. At sunrise the sun is low in the east and lights the underside of any high cloud from below; if a sheet of cirrus or cirrostratus is spreading in from the west while the eastern horizon is still clear, it glows red and orange. A red morning sky painted on high cloud is a front’s cloud arriving.

blocks.title: The countdown
points: Cirrus hooks spreading in from the west, long contrails that won’t go away: something is coming. Rain within a day or so.
A milky veil with a 22° halo, the sun still sharp: cirrostratus. Rain usually within 12 to 24 hours.
The sun a dim disc behind frosted glass, no shadows, no halo: altostratus. Rain within a few hours.
The sun gone, the base dark and blurred: nimbostratus, and steady rain.

blocks.text: The drawings in this lesson are clean; real skies are not. Here are this lesson’s veils in photographs, side by side with the clouds they are most often taken for, and the one thing that tells each pair apart. Keep these in mind for the check.

options.tell: Cirrus is threads with blue sky between them. Cirrostratus is the same ice spread into one veil over the whole sky, so thin you may notice it only by the whitened blue or a halo round the sun.

photos.cue: sun dim, as through frosted glass

options.tell: Look at the sun. Through cirrostratus it is still sharp-edged, things cast shadows, and there is often a halo. Through altostratus it is a dim, blurred disc, with no halo and no shadows.

photos.cue: sun still shows as a smudge

options.tell: Altostratus still lets the sun show as a smudge, and its base is high and smooth. Nimbostratus has thickened until the sun is gone, the base is low, dark and ragged, and rain or snow falls steadily.

blocks.text: First name the cloud types in the photos, and then say what these changing skies mean for the hours ahead.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Mares’ tails thickened into a milky veil with a halo; now the halo has faded and the sun is just a dim disc. When should you expect rain?
options: Not for days: high cloud like this passes over and leaves fair weather
Within the next several hours, as the sheet keeps lowering
In about a week, once the high cloud has had time to sink down
items.why: A progression from cirrus to cirrostratus and then to thickening altostratus marks an approaching warm front. Rain usually arrives within 12 to 24 hours of the first halo, and within just a few hours once altostratus dims the sun.

items.question: Patches of altocumulus at breakfast have merged into a grey sheet. By early afternoon the sun is a pale disc, as if behind frosted glass, and shadows have gone. What is the sky up to?
options: A frontal storm is coming: expect the sheet to lower into steady rain
Fair weather: the sheet will thin out and burn off by evening
Thunderstorms within the hour, building out of the grey sheet
items.why: A middle-floor sheet that keeps thickening is the broad, gentle lifting far out ahead of an approaching front. Altostratus thick enough to wipe out shadows usually lowers into steady rain within hours.

items.question: A few wispy streaks of cirrus have drifted across the blue sky all day without spreading or thickening, and contrails vanish quickly. What is the forecast?
options: A warm front arriving within hours, since cirrus always leads one
Thunderstorms by evening, as the ice falls into the warm air below
Fair weather for now: the high air is dry and nothing is building
items.why: Isolated wisps that stay isolated, and contrails that vanish, show dry high air with only a few moist pockets. Only cirrus that spreads and thickens into a veil warns of an approaching front.

items.question: A milky veil of cirrostratus produces a bright ring around the sun. Roughly how wide is the radius of that ring?
options: About a thumb’s width at arm’s length (2°)
About a spread hand at arm’s length (22°)
About halfway across the whole sky (90°)
items.why: Light passing through the 60° prism faces of hexagonal ice crystals bends by a minimum of 22°, which matches the span from thumb to little finger on an outstretched hand.

items.question: At sunrise, long contrails spread into a sheet and the high cloud in the west glows red. By ten the sun is still sharp but wears a ring. What now?
options: Fair weather: a red morning and a halo both mean dry, settled air
A thunderstorm by noon, as the ring is a sign of rising heaps
Rain likely within a day: a front’s high cloud is spreading in
items.why: Spreading contrails mean moist high air, the red sunrise is lighting high cloud arriving from the west, and the halo says cirrostratus. All three point to a warm front, with rain usually within 12 to 24 hours of the halo.

learned: Cirrus hooks (mares’ tails) are trails of falling ice crystals curved by wind shear. Cirrus that spreads and thickens from the west is a storm’s leading edge; a few wisps that stay a few wisps mean little.
Short contrails that vanish mean dry high air and fair weather; long ones that spread into a sheet mean moist high air ahead of a storm.
Six-sided ice crystals bend light by at least about 22°, piling it into a 22° halo, about a spread hand-span from the sun: the sign of a cirrostratus veil.
The sun is the gauge: sharp with shadows (cirrostratus), a dim disc behind frosted glass with no shadows (altostratus), or gone entirely (nimbostratus).

At a warm front, warm air glides up a gentle ramp over cold air, so its clouds arrive top first: cirrus, cirrostratus with a halo (rain within 12 to 24 hours), altostratus (a few hours), then nimbostratus and steady rain. A red sunrise on high cloud from the west says the same.

cirrus.title: Cirrus
cirrus.text: Detached, fibrous white filaments and hooked streaks (mares’ tails) on the high floor, formed by ice crystals falling through wind shear and sublimating in drier air below. Isolated cirrus that stays isolated indicates fair weather, whereas cirrus thickening and spreading across the sky from the west warns of an approaching front. Contrails say the same: short and vanishing in dry high air, long and spreading in moist.

cirrostratus.title: Cirrostratus
cirrostratus.text: A thin, whitish veil of ice crystals covering much or all of the high sky. The sun’s outline remains clear, ground shadows remain visible, and the layer frequently produces a 22° halo around the sun or moon. Thickening cirrostratus ahead of a warm front typically signals steady rain within 12 to 24 hours.

halo.title: The 22° halo
halo.text: Sunlight entering one side face of a hexagonal ice crystal and exiting two faces around passes through a 60° prism, bending by at least 22°. Millions of randomly tumbling crystals in cirrostratus concentrate refracted light right near that minimum angle, forming a bright ring of 22° radius (about a spread hand-span at arm’s length) around the sun or moon with a faintly reddish inner rim.

altostratus.title: Altostratus
altostratus.text: A uniform grey or bluish sheet of mixed droplets and ice crystals on the middle floor. The sun shines through dimly as if behind frosted glass, casting no shadows on the ground and producing no optical halo. It typically arrives as a thickening veil ahead of steady rain, with precipitation likely within a few hours.

warm-front.title: A warm front coming
warm-front.text: At a warm front, advancing warm air glides up over a retreating wedge of denser cold air along a gentle slope of roughly 1 in 100, forming layered clouds that extend up to a thousand kilometres ahead of the surface boundary. An observer sees the highest clouds first: cirrus hooks, then a cirrostratus veil with a 22° halo, then lowering altostratus that dims the sun, and finally deep nimbostratus bringing steady rain 12 to 24 hours after the halo.
